{{Short description|British physicist and author (1927–2019)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=September 2020}}
'''Desmond George King-Hele''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (3{{nbsp}}November 1927{{snd}}25{{nbsp}}December 2019)<ref name="Merchant" /> was a British [[physicist]], [[poet]] and author who crossed the divide between the arts and science to write extensively about the life of [[Erasmus Darwin]], whom he linked with the romantic poets [[Percy Bysshe Shelley|Shelley]], [[Wordsworth]], and [[Coleridge]]. In 1957, together with [[Doreen Gilmour]], and as part of the Guided Weapons department of [[Royal Aircraft Establishment]], he wrote a report proposing the use of the [[Blue Streak missile]] and [[Black Knight (rocket)|Black Knight]] as a satellite launcher.  See also: [[Blue Streak Satellite Launch Vehicle]].

==Life and career==
He was born in Seaford, Sussex, the son of Sidney G. and Bessie (née Sayer) King-Hele and was educated at [[Epsom College]]<ref name="Merchant">{{cite web|url=http://sounds.bl.uk/related-content/TRANSCRIPTS/021T-C1379X0013XX-0000A0.pdf|title=NATIONAL LIFE STORIES AN ORAL HISTORY OF BRITISH SCIENCE Desmond King-Hele Interviewed by Dr Paul Merchant|last=Merchant|first=Paul|date=15 March 2010|work=[[British Library]]|access-date=7 November 2012|quote=recommended me for a special scholarship to Epsom College, the large public school on the eastern outskirts of Epsom, and the college headmaster had agreed this.|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121007063019/sounds.bl.uk/related-content/TRANSCRIPTS/021T-C1379X0013XX-0000A0.pdf|archive-date=2012-10-07}}</ref> and [[Trinity College, Cambridge]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.bl.uk/voices-of-science/interviewees/desmond-king-hele |title=Desmond King-Hele - Voices of Science |website=The British Library |access-date=2018-12-21}}</ref>

He joined the [[Royal Aircraft Establishment]], Farnborough in 1948 and stayed there until 1988, researching the [[gravity of Earth]] and its [[upper atmosphere]] by [[satellite orbit determination]]. He was awarded the [[Eddington Medal]] of the [[Royal Astronomical Society]] in 1971 for his work on the [[geophysical]] application of the study of the [[orbit]]s of [[artificial satellite]]s. He was elected a [[fellow of the Royal Society]] in March 1966<ref>{{cite web |url=https://catalogues.royalsociety.org/CalmView/Record.aspx?src=CalmView.Persons&id=NA6215&pos=1 |title=Search past Fellows |work=royalsociety.org |access-date=2023-12-15}}</ref> and gave the [[Bakerian lecture]] in 1974 and the [[Wilkins Lecture]] in 1997.<ref>{{cite journal |title=The 1997 Wilkins Lecture: Erasmus Darwin, the Lunaticks and evolution |journal=Notes Rec. R. Soc. Lond. |volume=52 |issue=1 |pages=153–180 |date=1998 |doi=10.1098/rsnr.1998.0042 |last1=King-Hele |first1=D. |pmid=11619941 }}</ref> 2019 he was awarded an Honorary Doctor of Letters by the [[University of Derby]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.derby.ac.uk/about/honorary-awards/honorands/desmond-king-hele/ |title=Commendation |work=derby.ac.uk |access-date=2023-12-15}}</ref>

He is considered "one of the pioneers of [[space geodesy]]".<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1_68BAAAQBAJ&q=geodesy+Desmond+King-Hele&pg=PA68|title = Handbook of Satellite Orbits: From Kepler to GPS|isbn = 9783319034164|last1 = Capderou|first1 = Michel|date = 23 April 2014| publisher=Springer }}</ref>
Based on [[satellite geodesy]], King-Hele refined the estimate for [[Earth's pear shape]], finding a 45&nbsp;m difference between north and south polar radii.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=KING-HELE | first1=D. G. | last2=COOK | first2=G. E. | title=Refining the Earth's Pear Shape | journal=Nature | publisher=Springer Nature | volume=246 | issue=5428 | year=1973 | issn=0028-0836 | doi=10.1038/246086a0 | pages=86–88| bibcode=1973Natur.246...86K | s2cid=4260099 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=King-Hele |first=D. |date=1967 |title=The Shape of the Earth |journal=Scientific American |volume=217 |issue=4 |pages=67–80 |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican1067-67 |jstor=24926147|bibcode=1967SciAm.217d..67K }}</ref>

He married Marie Newman in 1954; they had two daughters.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://sounds.bl.uk/Oral-history/Science/021M-C1379X0013XX-0005V0 |title=King-Hele, Desmond (Part 5 of 21). An Oral History of British Science. - Oral history of British science - Oral history |website=sounds.bl.uk |access-date=2018-12-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210921060927/https://sounds.bl.uk/Oral-history/Science/021M-C1379X0013XX-0005V0 |archive-date=2021-09-21}}</ref>

He won the [[Chree medal and prize]] in 1971.

In 1973, he correctly predicted that [[Skylab]] would re-enter Earth's atmosphere in 1979.

King-Hele died on 25 December 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://announcements.telegraph.co.uk/deaths/238460/king-hele |title=King-Hele |work=The Telegraph  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200729025212/https://announcements.telegraph.co.uk/deaths/238460/king-hele |archive-date=2020-07-29}}</ref>

==Publications==

* ''Satellites and Scientific Research'' 1962
* ''Shelley: His Thought and Work'' 1962
* ''Erasmus Darwin'' 1963 
* ''Theory of Satellite Orbits in an Atmosphere'' 1964
* ''Doctor of Revolution'' 1977
* ''Observing Earth Satellites'' 1983
* ''Shelley: His Thought and Work'' 1984
* ''Erasmus Darwin and the Romantic Poets'' 1986
* ''A Tapestry of Orbits'' 1992, 2005
* ''Erasmus Darwin: A Life of Unequalled Achievement'' 1999
* ''Erasmus Darwin and Evolution'' 2014

He is also the author of two books of poetry, and of various articles published in journals, such as "Shelley and Science", ''Notes and Records of the Royal Society of London'', Vol. 46, No. 2 (Jul., 1992), pp.&nbsp;253–265.
